title: Vision Zero safety upgrades and sanitary sewer master plan
subtitle: Also covered: downtown event noise exemption, property standards by-law changes, and traffic calming budget review.
overview: The committee recommended a package of Vision Zero road safety measures {{vote:m3}}. It includes 2024 safety improvements, four new pedestrian crossovers, no-stopping zones near them, and a staff review of moving leftover formal traffic calming money into the Hot Spot program. Staff will report back through the 2025 Vision Zero update.

The committee also recommended approving the Integrated Sanitary Master Plan environmental study {{vote:m4}}. Staff said the sewer system can handle expected growth, but much of the work is repairing aging pipes and filling data gaps. The plan now goes to a 30-day public review.

On consent items, the committee recommended a noise exemption for downtown special events {{vote:m1}} and updates to the Property Standards By-law {{vote:m2}}. Because a special event is planned before the May 27 Council meeting, the noise exemption was to be forwarded to a Special Council meeting later that day. All of these are recommendations that Council must still adopt.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that staff carry out the 2024 Vision Zero safety improvements and receive the 2023 progress update.

The committee recommended Level 2 pedestrian crossovers at Belmont Avenue, Kingsway Drive at Greenfield Avenue, Park Street at Mount Hope Street, and Lawrence Avenue, with no-stopping zones and Uniform Traffic By-law changes.
The committee recommended that staff study moving the remaining formal traffic calming budget to the Vision Zero Hot Spot program and report back in the 2025 annual update.
The committee recommended approving the Schedule B environmental study report and filing it for the 30-day public review.
The committee recommended an exemption to the Noise by-law for all Downtown Special Events, which the report limits to the rest of 2024 with events ending by 11 p.m.
The committee recommended repealing and replacing specific sections of the Property Standards By-law and adding the updated rules to the Municipal Code.

debate: Delegates supporting Vision Zero urged a default 30 km/h speed limit, saying speed is the deciding factor in survival and injury. They also wanted wider use of automated speed enforcement, and one pointed to Wales as an example.

A delegate for the Active Transportation and Trails Advisory Committee asked Council to reinstate 30 km/h in all school zones at all times, including summer and evenings. They said schools serve as community hubs year-round.

Delegates also proposed school streets closed to cars around school start and end times, and narrower lanes. A school travel planning group described its pedestrian education program and said wider expansion would need more funding and instructors.

Staff said school zones are 30 km/h, or 40 km/h where automated enforcement is installed, and neighbourhood streets are 40 km/h. One councillor noted that injury and fatality numbers were similar before and after the 50-to-40 change, and staff said the fatalities were not in school zones.

On the budget amendment, staff said the Hot Spot program is more proactive and data-driven than formal traffic calming, which depends on resident requests. Several councillors supported it, and one said the formal process had been divisive.

On the sanitary plan, councillors asked about funding and development pressure. Staff said development charges might help pay for growth-related work and that pipes deteriorate with or without new development. Staff added that the roughly $75 million capital estimate is uncertain and that the highest-risk areas are those lacking condition data.
